addressed-iarc-027.title: GemNet: Universal Directional Graph Neural Networks for Molecules
addressed-iarc-027.summary: A zero Clebsch–Gordan factor removes interactions needed for the stated rotation-invariant scalar universality class. The spherical network gives identical outputs to a tetrahedron and its mirror, while a permitted scalar target changes sign.

checks.location: Appendix A Eq.13 claims that multiplying Clebsch-Gordan coefficients by the scalar C_(lf,0),(li,0)^(lo,0) does not affect model expressivity; Theorem 2 then claims universality for SO(3)-invariant scalar functions.
checks.claim: Appendix A Eq.13 claims that multiplying Clebsch-Gordan coefficients by the scalar C_(lf,0),(li,0)^(lo,0) does not affect model expressivity; Theorem 2 then claims universality for SO(3)-invariant scalar functions.
checks.explanation: The replacement multiplies each tensor-field coupling by an extra Clebsch–Gordan coefficient, which can vanish. This removes interactions that the original tensor product permits. The resulting spherical updates and scalar pooling also give identical outputs to mirror inputs, although the stated $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ target class includes scalars that change sign under reflection.
checks.demonstration:
For $l_f=l_i=l_o=1$, the extra factor $C^{(1,0)}_{(1,0),(1,0)}$ vanishes, whereas the $1\otimes1\to1$ coupling is nonzero: in Cartesian coordinates it is the cross product. Multiplying that coupling by zero removes it.

The obstruction persists through the entire spherical network. By the spherical-harmonic addition theorem, the filter in Equation (3) depends on its two directions only through their dot product. Hence, for every $Q\in\mathrm{O}(3)$,
$$F_{\mathrm{sphere}}(Qx,Q\hat r)=F_{\mathrm{sphere}}(x,\hat r).$$
The input features are scalar, so induction through Equation (3) gives $H_{QX}(\hat r)=H_X(Q^\top\hat r)$. Changing variables in the spherical integral of Equation (4) therefore gives identical scalar outputs on $X$ and $QX$.

Now let the three feature rows $H_{1j},H_{2j},H_{3j}$ distinguish three neighbor types, and define
$$v_r(a)=\sum_jH_{rj}(X_j-X_a),\qquad y_a(X,H)=\det\bigl(v_1(a),v_2(a),v_3(a)\bigr).$$
This is a degree-$6$ polynomial in $(X,H)$. Relative coordinates make it translation invariant; simultaneous relabeling of positions and features makes its node outputs permutation equivariant; and $\det Q=1$ makes it invariant under $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. Take a center at $0$, neighbors at $e_1,e_2,e_3$, and one-hot type features on those neighbors. Then $y_a=1$. Reflection by $Q=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1)$ gives $y_a=-1$. A spherical network has the same output $z$ on both, and thus
$$\max\{|z-1|,|z+1|\}\geq1.$$
It cannot approximate this permitted continuous target uniformly on the compact set containing the tetrahedron and its mirror. This disproves both the polynomial and continuous-universality clauses of Theorem 2.
checks.repair:
Retaining the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ target class requires parity-odd interactions, including $1\otimes1\to1$, that Equation (13) discards. A sufficient replacement is a full equivariant polynomial model: center the coordinates, allow products of coordinate and invariant-feature channels, and project the resulting polynomials onto the required rotation and permutation symmetries. For any polynomial target with those symmetries, this projection returns the target itself. For a continuous target, approximate it by polynomials on the compact union of the input set's rotation and permutation orbits; averaging the approximant over those symmetries cannot increase its uniform error. This establishes the two desired guarantees for the replacement class. It is a substantial architectural replacement, not a correction to the scalar multiplier alone.

Changing $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ to $\mathrm{O}(3)$ removes the chiral target but does not supply the missing universality proof. A theorem restricted to fixed features and reflection-even targets still needs a valid proof. [The Price of Freedom, Proposition 3.2 and Appendix K](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/xie25c.html) derives the same missing odd-degree interactions; it does not provide that proof or a GemNet erratum.
checks.scope: The witness uses invariant type features, distinct points, a full-rank tetrahedron and a scalar polynomial target. The full-span assumption of Theorem 3 does not restrict Theorem 2. The result concerns the stated universality class; it does not establish a failure on reflection-even molecular-energy targets.
checks.title: Reflection invariance prevents the claimed universality for rotation-invariant scalar targets
checks.claimContext: Appendix A, Equation (13), replaces the tensor-field-network Clebsch–Gordan coupling by the spherical-product coupling below and claims that this preserves expressivity. Theorem 2 then claims universality for scalar targets invariant under translations and $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ rotations and equivariant under permutations. Here $C$ denotes a Clebsch–Gordan coefficient; $l_i,l_f,l_o$ are the input, filter and output harmonic degrees, and $m_i,m_f,m_o$ are their corresponding orders.
checks.contextBefore: The spherical network multiplies scalar functions on $S^2$ by radial-and-angular filters and integrates over the sphere for scalar output. Its universality proof transfers a tensor-field-network result through an asserted equivalence of the two feature spaces.
checks.whyItMatters: Theorem 2 transfers universality from tensor field networks to the spherical architecture. Its permitted targets include a scalar that distinguishes a tetrahedron from its mirror. An architecture that gives both inputs the same output cannot meet that guarantee.
checks.verificationNote: The central scalar-universality guarantee fails on a permitted reflection-odd target, not only at an intermediate proof step.
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3, Eqs. (3)-(4) and Theorem 2, PDF p.4; Appendix A, Eqs. (12)-(16), PDF p.14

addressed-iarc-027.issueTitle: A zero Clebsch-Gordan coefficient invalidates the spherical-product equivalence
addressed-iarc-027.plainExplanation: Appendix A treats multiplication by a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient as preserving expressivity, but that coefficient is zero when the three angular degrees sum to an odd number. This removes interactions needed by some SO(3)-invariant scalar functions. The Price of Freedom independently derives the same selection rule for spherical products; it does not present a GemNet erratum.

checks.claim: For every m <= 2^{sqrt d -1}, Pr[span(S1)=span(S2)] = exp(-Omega(sqrt d)), and the sum/intersection dimension gap is Omega(sqrt d) with constant probability.
checks.explanation: The missing sample-size lower bound is essential, not a constant adjustment.
checks.demonstration: For $m=1$, the dimension gap is at most two for every distribution, so it cannot be order $\sqrt d$ with constant probability. For the displayed construction the exact agreement probability is $(1-4^{-k})/(3k)+4^{-k}$, which is polynomial rather than exponentially small in $k$.
checks.repair: Restrict to $k\le m\le2^{k-1}$. Choose block $j=\lfloor\log_2(m/k)\rfloor+1$, whose per-vector mass $r$ obeys $1/(2m)\le r\le1/m$. The missing probability $q=(1-r)^m$ lies in $[1/4,3/4]$. If $X$ counts differing occupancies in this block across two samples, then $\mathbb EX=2kq(1-q)\ge3k/8$ and $X\le k$, giving $\Pr(X\ge3k/16)\ge3/13$. For agreement, condition on the first occupied subset $A$. If $|A|\le k/2$, the second sample must avoid missing mass at least $k/(4m)$, with probability at most $e^{-k/4}$. If $|A|>k/2$, it must hit every member of $A$. Poissonizing its size to mean $2m$ gives independent occupancies with hit probability at most $1-e^{-2}$; monotonicity and $\Pr(\operatorname{Pois}(2m)\ge m)\ge1/2$ bound the fixed-size probability by $2(1-e^{-2})^{k/2}$. This proves both restricted conclusions without assuming independence of fixed-size occupancies.
checks.scope: The repair establishes the proposition on the restricted range. It does not recover the original small-sample quantifier.
checks.title: The lower-bound proposition cannot include arbitrarily small samples

checks.location: Appendix D Step5 / Section3.2 quantization bound
checks.claim: this yields the worst-case bound $\delta\theta\lesssim 0.78^{\circ}$ for $b{=}8$
checks.explanation: Near identity, the inverse stereographic map changes the quaternion vector by twice the code error, and physical rotation angle supplies another factor of two. The derivation drops one of those factors.
checks.demonstration:
The inverse stereographic map is

\[
q_w=\frac{1-\|S\|^2}{1+\|S\|^2},\qquad q_{xyz}=\frac{2S}{1+\|S\|^2}.
\]

At identity \(S=0\), nearest rounding to \(2^b\) evenly spaced levels on \([-1,1]\) puts each coordinate at \(\pm1/(2^b-1)\). The exact resulting physical rotation error is

\[
\delta\theta=4\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2^b-1}\right).
\]

It equals \(1.5566694125^\circ\) for 8 bits and \(0.0060571726^\circ\) for 16 bits. Any nearest tie-breaking has the same norm, and nearby non-tie inputs approach the same error. These errors cannot be removed by a nonidentity hexagonal crystal symmetry: the nearest nontrivial proper rotation is separated by at least \(60^\circ\).
checks.repair: Use the local coefficient \(4\|\delta S\|\). A valid global bound under ordinary componentwise nearest rounding is \(\delta\theta\leq4\|\delta S\|\leq4\sqrt3/(2^b-1)\) radians: the inverse stereographic sphere differential has norm factor \(2/(1+\|S\|^2)\leq2\), and physical rotation distance is at most twice quaternion-sphere distance. This gives \(1.5566933518^\circ\) and \(0.0060571726^\circ\), respectively.
checks.scope: The counterexample violates the stated worst-case physical rotation bounds. A worst-case bound and the separately reported mean round-trip error are different quantities.

checks.location: Proposition 4.1 Eq. (4.2); Theorem 4.2 Eq. (4.4); proof B.11 Eq. (B.37) and B.7 Eq. (B.5)
checks.claim: Randomized block DCA with arbitrary allowed block convex subgradients satisfies a vanishing full Clarke-stationarity residual.
checks.explanation: Separately valid block subgradients need not be coordinates of a single full subgradient. Equation (B.37) assembles those independent choices as though they formed a full Clarke subgradient. A block update can therefore stop even when the full residual remains positive.
checks.demonstration:
On \(\mathbb R^2\), take
\[f(x,y)=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}+\min(x,y)=g(x,y)-h(x,y),\]
\[g(x,y)=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2},\qquad h(x,y)=\max(-x,-y),\]
and use these functions as the block decompositions. Both parts are convex in every block; \(g\) has globally \(1\)-Lipschitz block gradients, and \(h\) is globally \(1\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm. The full domain is open, and all required block minimizers exist.

Initialize at \((0,0)\). Holding the other coordinate fixed at zero gives \(\partial_x h(0,0)=\partial_y h(0,0)=[-1,0]\), so the independent choices \(u_x=u_y=0\) are allowed. Each exact block model is then \(z^2/2\) up to a constant, and each proximal model is \((1+\rho)z^2/2\). Both have unique minimizer zero. Thus every possible random block sequence leaves the iterate at \((0,0)\) forever.

The full Clarke subdifferential is nevertheless
\[\partial_C f(0,0)=\operatorname{conv}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}.\]
Its nearest point to zero is \((1/2,1/2)\), giving \(\mathcal G^2(0,0)=1/2\). Also \(f^*=-1/2\), attained at \((-1,0)\) and \((0,-1)\), so the initial objective gap is \(1/2\).

Use the admissible constants \(n=2\), \(L=R=1\), \(H=1/2\), \(E=1\) and \(\rho=4\). Generalized smoothness holds with constant subquadratic function \(\ell\equiv1\). The chosen positive \(H\) bounds the zero increment of \(h\) along the constant iterates, and \(E^2=2LH=1\); the required proximal condition \(\rho\ge2L(E+R)/E\) holds with equality. At \(K=100\), the two claimed residual upper bounds are
\[\frac{2Ln(f(0)-f^*)}{K}=\frac1{50},\qquad \frac{2(L+\rho)n(f(0)-f^*)}{K}=\frac1{10}.\]
Both are smaller than the actual squared residual \(1/2\). The failure comes from assembling incompatible block choices: zero belongs to both partial subdifferentials of \(h\), but \((0,0)\) does not belong to its full subdifferential.
checks.repair:
Before drawing the random block, require compatible candidate choices: the assembled vector \(z=(\nabla_i g_i-u_i)_i\) must belong to \(\partial_C f\). On the unconstrained subclass with globally \(L\)-Lipschitz gradients of the smooth block parts, compare each exact surrogate minimizer with the trial step \(-z_i/(L+\rho)\). This gives
\[f(\theta)-\mathbb E_k f(\theta^+)\ge\frac{\|z\|^2}{2n(L+\rho)}\ge\frac{\mathcal G(\theta)^2}{2n(L+\rho)}.\]
Telescoping yields the residual rate for this restricted algorithm.

A common global decomposition \(f=g-h\), with smooth \(g\) and convex \(h\), supplies compatible choices by selecting one full \(v\in\partial h\) and using its coordinates for all \(u_i\). In the construction, \(v=(-1/2,-1/2)\) makes the selected coordinate move to \(-1/10\) at \(\rho=4\); the actual decrease is \(19/200\), exceeding the trial-step lower bound \(1/40\). General BDC decompositions with arbitrary independent block choices need not have this compatibility. The restricted correction therefore does not establish the advertised wider guarantee. Replacing full Clarke stationarity by coordinatewise criticality would instead weaken the target.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns the full Clarke-stationarity guarantees for arbitrary block subgradient selections, including the exact and proximal deterministic algorithms. The structural representation results are not assessed.
checks.title: Independent block subgradients need not give a Clarke-stationary iterate
checks.whyItMatters: The algorithm may remain forever at a point with positive full Clarke residual, even for a smooth quadratic minus a Lipschitz convex function. Proximal regularization alone does not remove that fixed point.
checks.claimContext: Section 4 defines the full Clarke residual \(\mathcal G(\theta)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C f(\theta))\). Proposition 4.1 bounds it for randomized block DCA with arbitrary allowed block subgradients; Theorem 4.2 gives a proximal counterpart.
checks.verificationNote: Checked against arXiv v1, uploaded 19 April 2026.
checks.checkedLocation: arXiv v1 · Section 4, PDF pages 8–10; Proposition 4.1, Theorem 4.2; Appendix B.11, Eq. (B.37)

checks.claim: \operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^{k})=\frac{\tau{\bm{F}}^{-1}y+x^{k}}{\tau{\bm{M}}+I},
checks.explanation: The mask is diagonal in Fourier coordinates, not image coordinates. Dividing an image-domain numerator by its diagonal does not solve the stated proximal problem, even when the data vanish outside the mask.
checks.demonstration:
Take the two-point unitary Fourier transform, sampling mask and data

\[
F=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
M=\operatorname{diag}(1,0),\quad x^k=0,\quad y=(1,0)^T,\quad\tau=1.
\]

The unique proximal minimizer must solve

\[
(I+\tau F^*MF)u=x^k+\tau F^*My.
\]

Its solution is \(u=(1/(2\sqrt2),1/(2\sqrt2))^T\). Equation (18) instead gives \((1/(2\sqrt2),1/\sqrt2)^T\), which fails this normal equation. Here \(My=y\), so the failure is entirely the placement of the denominator.
checks.repair:
Transform the normal equation to Fourier coordinates and divide there:

\[
\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k)
=F^*\left(\frac{Fx^k+\tau My}{1+\tau m}\right),
\]

where \(m\) is the binary diagonal of \(M\). Unitarity gives \(F(I+\tau F^*MF)F^*=I+\tau M\), proving the expression. If \(My=y\), the numerator simplifies accordingly. A full mask is a special case where the printed denominator commutes with \(F^*\).
checks.scope: Equation (18) fails as a general MRI proximal map because the mask is diagonal in Fourier coordinates. Equation (16)’s gradient and the spatial inpainting map are separate formulas.
checks.claimContext: Appendix D.4.1 defines \(f(x,y)=\tfrac12\|MFx-y\|_2^2\), with unitary Fourier transform \(F\) and binary Fourier mask \(M\). Equation (18) gives this componentwise image-domain formula.
checks.title: The MRI proximal denominator belongs inside the inverse Fourier transform
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed closed-form quadratic solver is wrong for general undersampled MRI masks.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix D.4.1, Eq. (18) (arXiv v2)

checks.claim: the partial derivative with respect to the second argument vanishes at the exact fixed point.
checks.explanation: Equal state values make the inertial displacement zero, but do not make its derivative with respect to one independently varied state zero.
checks.demonstration:
Write \(G(x)=x-\tau\nabla F(x)\), \(\beta=1-\alpha\), so \(T(x_1,x_2)=G((1+\beta)x_1-\beta x_2)\). At a diagonal equilibrium,

\[
D_1T=(1+\beta)DG(x^*),\qquad D_2T=-\beta DG(x^*).
\]

Take zero data term, \(\lambda=1\), and the constant denoiser network \(N_\theta(x)=\theta\), giving the smooth energy \(F(x;\theta)=g_\theta(x)=\tfrac12(x-\theta)^2\). Choose \(\tau=1/4\), \(\alpha=1/2\) and \(x^*=\theta\). Then

\[
D_1T=9/8,\qquad D_2T=-3/8\ne0.
\]

The full implicit equation gives \(\partial_\theta x^*=(1/4)/(1-9/8+3/8)=1\), as required. Omitting the second partial would give \(-2\).
checks.repair: Replace the vanishing claim by \(D_2T=-(1-\alpha)(I-\tau\nabla^2F(x^*))\), and retain \(D_1T+D_2T=DG(x^*)\) in implicit differentiation. The chain rule proves both equalities. When \(I-DG(x^*)\) is invertible, this reduces to the usual one-state equilibrium sensitivity. The same remark's parameter derivatives do vanish: \(\partial_\tau T=-\nabla F(x^*)=0\), and \(\partial_\alpha T=-DG(x^*)(x_1-x_2)=0\).
checks.scope: This repairs one false assertion in Remark 6. The preceding exact implicit-derivative equation is correct, and the declared Jacobian-free approximation is not shown ineffective by this witness.
checks.claimContext: Remark 6 states that the partial derivative of the two-state i-DEQ operator with respect to its second state argument vanishes at an exact fixed point.
checks.title: An inertial state derivative need not vanish at equilibrium
checks.whyItMatters: Discarding this state derivative can change the exact equilibrium sensitivity. The preceding two-state implicit formula correctly keeps it.
checks.checkedLocation: Appendix D.2.2, Remark 6 (arXiv v2)

checks.claim:
Under Assumptions 3.1, Algorithm 1,
satisfy after at most $n$ iterations,
checks.explanation: Those smoothness properties do not ensure stability for the printed parameter range. The cited RISP theorem couples step size, momentum, restart threshold and epoch length to curvature, accuracy and total iteration budget; those restrictions are absent from the proposition.
checks.demonstration:
Use the actual nonnegative energy model: \(f(x)=2x^2\), corresponding to forward operator \(A=2\) and data zero, and identity denoiser \(N(x)=x\), so \(g(x)=\tfrac12|x-N(x)|^2=0\). The gradient is \(4x\), the Hessian is constant, and all stated smoothness assumptions hold. Choose \(\tau=0.75\), \(\alpha=0.5\), \(B=1\), and \(x^{-1}=x^0=1\).

At every restart state \(a\), the extrapolated first point is \(a\), giving

\[
x^+=a-0.75(4a)=-2a,\qquad |x^+-a|^2=9a^2>B^2.
\]

The restart sets the new initial state to \(-2a\) and resets the local counter. Inductively the restart values are \((-2)^j\), with gradient norms \(4\cdot2^j\). The printed loop never reaches its output stage; even an added total-step cap cannot make these gradients decrease. The example also has \(\tau<1\), so the general claim also fails under that optional restriction.
checks.repair:
A specific supported restricted statement is available in RISP Theorem 1. For the full energy use \(L=L_f+\lambda L_g\), \(\rho=\rho_f+\lambda\rho_g\), finite gap \(\Delta_F=F(x^0)-\inf F\), and its gradient-field and regularity hypotheses. Run that theorem's algorithm and output convention with

\[
\tau=\frac1{4L},\quad B=\sqrt{\varepsilon/\rho},\quad
\alpha=4(\varepsilon\rho\tau^2)^{1/4}\in(0,1),\quad K=\alpha^{-1},
\]

and

\[
\varepsilon=2^{4/7}\Delta_F^{4/7}L^{2/7}\rho^{1/7}n^{-4/7}+L^2\rho^{-1}n^{-4}.
\]

Use its final-epoch averaged output \(\widehat z=(K_0+1)^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{K_0}z^k\), where \(K_0\) minimizes \(\|x^{k+1}-x^k\|\) over \(\lfloor K/2\rfloor\leq k\leq K-1\), and count all restart epochs in the total budget. Its conclusion is \(\|\nabla F(\widehat z)\|\leq82\varepsilon=O(n^{-4/7})\). This invokes the cited theorem with its conditions, rather than proving the rate for arbitrary Algorithm 1 parameters.

A modest independently proved alternative sets inertia to zero, \(\alpha=1\), and takes gradient descent with \(\tau\leq1/L\). Summing the descent lemma gives

\[
\min_{k<n}\|\nabla F(x_k)\|\leq
\sqrt{\frac{2(F(x_0)-\inf F)}{\tau n}}.
\]

That modified algorithm has the usual \(O(n^{-1/2})\) certificate.
checks.scope: The repairs are a specifically scheduled cited algorithm or an explicitly modified gradient-descent algorithm, not a new accelerated guarantee for learned hyperparameters. The small-gradient output statement does not itself imply convergence of every raw iterate to a single point.

checks.claim: Perron radius below9 is sufficient for isolated inhibitory Schur stability.
checks.explanation: The Perron eigenvalue tests only one mode. A nonnegative matrix can also have negative eigenvalues, which the inhibitory minus sign turns into expanding modes.
checks.demonstration:
Take strictly positive symmetric weights and their tangent matrix:

\[W_{II}=\begin{pmatrix}0.1&6.9\\6.9&0.1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \operatorname{spec}(W_{II})=\{7,-6.8\},\qquad\operatorname{spec}(0.8I-0.2W_{II})=\{-0.6,2.16\}.\]

The Perron value is below 9 and equals the target 7, but the tangent is unstable. With frozen drive \(u_I=8\mathbf1\), \(r_I^*=\mathbf1\) is a strictly active ReLU fixed point. Small perturbations in direction \((1,-1)\) grow by 2.16. Zero cross blocks and eight passive excitatory coordinates give an 80:20 embedding.
checks.repair:
The exact condition checks every eigenvalue:

\[|0.8-0.2\lambda_j(W_{II})|<1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad |\lambda_j(W_{II})-4|<5.\]

checks.demonstration:

\[x^\top(DH+H^\top D)x=2(\rho-1)v^\top D_Ev\ge0\quad\text{when }\rho\ge1.\]

Use an appropriate stability condition for the actual matrix. Ordinary feedback stabilization is possible: take

\[W_{\mathrm{eff}}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-3\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad H=\begin{pmatrix}1&-3\\1&-2\end{pmatrix},\quad P=\begin{pmatrix}6&-7\\-7&11\end{pmatrix}\succ0.\]

checks.location: PropositionC.7(ii), Moore-Osgood argument, RemarkC.8 raw estimator
checks.claim: Positive perturbation continuity guarantees Perron convergence for the raw reducible estimator and any simultaneous vanishing-perturbation/increasing-iteration limit.
checks.explanation: For each fixed positive perturbation the iteration converges, but this does not imply raw reducible convergence or uniform convergence as the perturbation disappears. A periodic component supplies an explicit failure with every normalization defined.
checks.demonstration:
Take

\[W=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&0\\1/2&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\rho(W)=1,\qquad\widehat\lambda(W;K)=\begin{cases}5/4&K\ge2\text{ even},\\4/5&K\text{ odd}.\end{cases}\]

The raw estimator oscillates. For a joint-limit witness set \(\varepsilon_m=10^{-2m}\), \(K_m=2m\). Since \(\|W_\varepsilon\|_\infty\le2.3\) for \(\varepsilon\le0.1\),

\[\|W_\varepsilon^k-W^k\|_\infty\le3k\varepsilon(2.3)^{k-1}.\]

At \(k=2m,2m+1\) the bound tends to zero. The sum-ratio denominator stays bounded below, so the perturbed estimate tends to \(5/4\), although \(\rho(W_{\varepsilon_m})\to1\).
checks.repair:
A fixed diagonal shift gives a corrected estimator for every fixed finite nonnegative \(W\). Fix \(c>0\), put \(A=W+cI\), and use

\[v_0=\mathbf1/n,\qquad v_{k+1}=\frac{Av_k}{\|Av_k\|_2},\qquad \widetilde\rho_K=\frac{\mathbf1^\top Wv_K}{\mathbf1^\top v_K}=\frac{\mathbf1^\top Av_K}{\mathbf1^\top v_K}-c.\]

The final numerator can therefore use the original matrix \(W\); only the iteration products need the shift. Every normalization is defined because \(Av\ge cv>0\) for positive iterates.

To prove consistency, write \(R=\rho(W)+c>0\). For every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(W\),

\[|\lambda+c|\le|\lambda|+c\le\rho(W)+c=R.\]

Equality requires \(\lambda=\rho(W)\), so \(R\) is the only eigenvalue value of \(A\) on its spectral circle. Jordan expansion of \(a_k=\mathbf1^\top A^k\mathbf1\) gives

\[a_k=R^k\bigl(P(k)+o(1)\bigr),\]

where \(P\) is a real polynomial and all other eigenvalue contributions are exponentially smaller times polynomials. Choose a nonzero nonnegative Perron vector \(u\le\mathbf1\). Positivity yields \(a_k\ge R^k\mathbf1^\top u\), so \(P\) is nonzero. Since \(a_k>0\), its leading coefficient is positive. Repeated or defective Perron eigenvalues merely change the polynomial degree. Hence

\[\widetilde\rho_K=\frac{a_{K+1}}{a_K}-c\longrightarrow R-c=\rho(W).\]

The original ordered positive-perturbation limit also remains valid:

\[\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\lim_{K\to\infty}\widehat\lambda(W_\varepsilon;K)=\rho(W).\]

That ordered limit does not establish the original unshifted estimator’s convergence; the fixed-shift procedure is a modification that restores the same radius target.
checks.scope:
The displayed counterexample still refutes the original unshifted iteration and arbitrary joint perturbation limit. The fixed-shift modification gives pointwise asymptotic consistency for each fixed nonnegative \(W\) and fixed \(c>0\), including reducible, periodic, nilpotent and zero matrices.

It supplies no uniform finite-iteration accuracy bound. For \(W=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the corrected estimate is \(c/(K+2c)\), so convergence is only of order \(1/K\). A shift allowed to vanish with \(K\) can retain the periodic obstruction. Pointwise consistency does not justify an arbitrary joint limit or the original fixed iteration count.
checks.whyItMatters: A fixed diagonal shift preserves the target Perron radius and restores asymptotic consistency for every nonnegative matrix; the original unshifted guarantee still fails.
checks.claimContext: Proposition C.7(ii) uses \(W_\varepsilon=W+\varepsilon\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\), then extends convergence to any joint \(\varepsilon\downarrow0,K\to\infty\) limit. Remark C.8 relies on it for the unperturbed reducible estimator with uniform initialization.
checks.title: Positive perturbation does not justify the raw Perron iteration

checks.claim: Equality of Perron spectral radius and operator2-norm characterizes normal nonnegative matrices.
checks.explanation: Normality is sufficient for equality, but is not necessary. The converse fails even for strictly positive matrices within the primitive Perron setting.
checks.demonstration:
Take

\[W=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.3&0.2\\0.2&0.4&0.4\\0.3&0.3&0.4\end{pmatrix}.\]

All row and column sums equal 1, so \(W\mathbf1=\mathbf1\) and

\[1=\rho(W)\le\|W\|_2\le\sqrt{\|W\|_1\|W\|_\infty}=1.\]

Yet \(WW^\top\ne W^\top W\); their difference has Frobenius norm approximately \(0.0489898\). Thus equality holds for a nonnormal, strictly positive matrix.
checks.repair: Keep the universal inequality \(\rho(W)\le\|W\|_2\) and the sufficient implication from normality to equality. Nonnegative matrices with equal constant row and column sums form another sufficient equality class and can be nonnormal. Symmetric positive matrices provide the usual normal equality control.
checks.scope: Only the necessity of normality is false. The underlying spectral-radius inequality, normal-matrix equality, and Perron convergence under the proposition’s separate primitive hypotheses are unaffected.
checks.title: Norm equality does not characterize normality
checks.whyItMatters: This is an ancillary characterization error; norm equality alone cannot diagnose normality or symmetric recurrence.

review-neurips-2026-152525.title: Calibration without Ground Truth

checks.claim: Compatibility defined by calibration of h(Q1) yields a convex set, so Eq2 projection universally improves proper loss.
checks.explanation: Calibration constraints can be linear for a fixed partition of reports, but applying $h$ may merge reports and change that partition. The resulting set $\mathcal H_{\rm comp}$ need not be convex. The Bregman projection argument in Appendix A.2 therefore does not apply to the printed feasible set, and its chosen transformation can increase loss.
checks.demonstration:
Use binary outcomes and identify a forecast with its probability of $Y=1$. Let the primary report $Q_1$ be $0.49$ or $0.51$, each with probability $1/2$, with
$$\Pr(Y=1\mid Q_1=0.49)=0.2,\qquad \Pr(Y=1\mid Q_1=0.51)=0.8.$$
Set $Q_0=Y$. The reference is perfectly calibrated. Because its reports are zero and one, reference calibration forces $Y=Q_0$ in every outcome extension compatible with the observed joint law of $(Q_0,Q_1)$. There is thus no alternative extension that could change the two displayed conditional probabilities. The primary predictor is not mutually calibrated with this reference.

Write $h$ as the pair of its outputs at $0.49,0.51$. If it keeps the reports distinct, calibration forces $h=(0.2,0.8)$. If it pools them, calibration forces $h=(0.5,0.5)$. These exhaust the two possible partitions, so
$$\mathcal H_{\rm comp}=\{(0.2,0.8),(0.5,0.5)\}.$$
Its midpoint $(0.35,0.65)$ is not compatible, contradicting the convexity asserted in Observation 3.2.

Take the differentiable strictly proper loss $\ell(p,y)=(p-y)^2$, with divergence $D_\ell(p,q)=(p-q)^2$. Let $h_{\rm sep}$ and $h_{\rm pool}$ denote the distinct-output and pooled maps. The projection objective values are exactly
$$\mathbb E D_\ell(h_{\rm sep}(Q_1),Q_1)=\frac{841}{10000},\qquad \mathbb E D_\ell(h_{\rm pool}(Q_1),Q_1)=\frac1{10000}.$$ Thus Eq. (2) uniquely selects the pooled forecast $0.5$.

The original expected loss is $2441/10000$, while pooling gives $1/4$. Hence the actual improvement is
$$\frac{2441}{10000}-\frac14=-\frac{59}{10000},$$
whereas Theorem 3.3 claims it is at least $1/10000$. The transformation increases loss despite finite supports, a calibrated reference and a differentiable strictly proper loss. The failure concerns which compatible transformation the printed objective selects; the unpooled conditional forecast does improve the example.
checks.repair:
Define compatibility at the original report, rather than only after reports may have been pooled. Require an extension of the observed forecast-pair law satisfying
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf Y\mid Q_0]=Q_0,\qquad \mathbb E[\mathbf Y\mid Q_1]=h(Q_1),$$
where $\mathbf Y$ is the one-hot outcome vector. This is a stronger feasible-set definition.

For finite report supports, write $p_{ab}=\Pr(Q_0=a,Q_1=b)$ and introduce joint masses $t_{aby}\ge0$. Impose
$$\sum_y t_{aby}=p_{ab},\qquad \sum_b t_{aby}=\Pr(Q_0=a)a_y,$$
and, for reports with positive probability, set
$$h(b)_y=\frac{\sum_a t_{aby}}{\Pr(Q_1=b)}.$$
These linear constraints define a probability polytope, whose image in $h$ is compact and convex. It contains the true conditional forecast $r(b)=\mathbb E[\mathbf Y\mid Q_1=b]$ for every extension with a calibrated reference, and uses the observed forecast-pair distribution without requiring outcome labels.

Under the theorem's differentiability conditions, projection onto this corrected set gives the Bregman inequality
$$\mathbb E[D_\ell(r,Q_1)-D_\ell(r,h^*)]\ge\mathbb E D_\ell(h^*,Q_1).$$
The left-hand side is the proper-loss improvement, so this establishes the intended uniform lower bound for the corrected feasible set. In the example that set contains only $(0.2,0.8)$, giving loss $4/25$ and improvement $841/10000$, equal to its projection distance. This correction does not make the original pooled-output set convex; it replaces that set by a stronger report-conditioned one.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns Observation 3.2 and the guarantee for Eq. (2)'s minimizer as defined. It does not refute existence of an improving transformation: the unpooled conditional forecast improves the example, and the corrected convex projection gives the general argument.
checks.whyItMatters: The printed projection can worsen even squared loss when its reference is perfect. Conditioning compatibility on the original report restores a convex feasible set and the intended improvement argument.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 3.3 uses the projection $h^*$ in Eq. (2) onto transformations whose outputs are mutually calibrated with the reference. It claims a uniform proper-loss reduction when the original predictors are not mutually calibrated.
checks.title: Pooling reports breaks convexity and can increase loss
checks.checkedLocation: Section 3.2.1, Observation 3.2; Equation (2); Theorem 3.3; Appendix A.2

Equations 1–47, weighted reconstruction and rank allocation, PDE/Sobolev metrics and trace energy balancing.

checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. Verified the positive-definite weighted-SVD derivation algebraically and numerically. The cross term from the Frobenius expansion is exactly -2Tr(LWprime Sigma_cov W^T L^T), and invertible left/right transformations preserve rank. The screening objection correctly identifies that an undamped PSD square root cannot be ordinarily inverted. However, the implementation paragraph explicitly adds epsilon I before the EVD fallback, making a consistent damped interpretation possible. An undamped interpretation can also be repaired by operating on the supported ranges; the diagonal rank-deficient example has an exact zero-loss rank-one solution via pseudoinverses. Consequently no false mathematical conclusion is not refuted by this check all reasonable readings in the examined material. Exact equivalence to the original undamped objective is not certified, and damping changes the metric in general.

$$\mathbb E[(A-q)(\widehat m-m)\mid\text{training data}]=o_p(n^{-1/2}).$$
At the target, the score difference is exactly $-(A-q)(\widehat m-m)$. The drift condition controls its mean. Conditional independence of a held-out fold and its nuisance fit, boundedness of $q$, and $L_2$ consistency make the centered empirical difference $o_p(n^{-1/2})$. Increasing \(M\) reduces only the logarithmic term, so the proof does not obtain its required constant testing-error probability. There is also a range obstruction under Assumption 1: every admissible pair has joint Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence at most \(HG\). Choosing \(n\) large enough for the sample-size condition and \(\varepsilon\le1\) does not change the Fano expression: \[1-\frac{100}{32}-\frac{\log2}{\log16}=-\frac{19}{8}=-2.375.\] It is not at least \(1/2\), and its limit as \(M\to\infty\) is \(-17/8\). Thus a larger class cannot justify the last inequality. Separately, let \(\pi^\star\) be the data-generating policy and \(P^\pi\) the joint trajectory law of a candidate \(\pi\). Assumption 1 bounds each conditional log ratio from \(\pi^\star\) to \(\pi\) by \(G\), so \[\log\frac{P^{\pi^\star}(S)}{P^\pi(S)}\le HG,\qquad \operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi^\star}\|P^\pi)\le HG.\] This holds for every candidate returned by a selector, for every realized training sample. Consequently its expected KL risk, and hence the minimax risk over such selectors, is at most \(HG\). Corollary 1 claims absolute constants \(c,c_0>0\) giving a lower bound \(cH^2G^2\log M/n\) for every \(n\ge c_0\log M\) and every \(H\). Given any such constants, set \(G=1\), \(M=4\), \(n=\max\{1,\lceil c_0\log4\rceil\}\) and choose an integer \(H>n/(c\log4)\). The claimed lower bound exceeds \(H\), contradicting the upper bound. The uniform-horizon rate also needs a revised statement and a new proof: capping a proposed lower bound at \(HG\), or restricting the range to \(n\ge cHG\log M\), removes the range contradiction but does not fix the Fano argument. For \(0<G\leq1\), a weaker lower bound follows from \(\varepsilon=(G/4)\sqrt{\log M/n}\), \(M\ge4\) and \(n\ge\log M\). Choose a power of two \(d\) with \(d-1\ge M\); the nonconstant columns of a \(d\)-dimensional Hadamard matrix supply \(M\) balanced, pairwise orthogonal sign vectors \(v\). On tokens \(s\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), define \(P_v(s)=e^{\varepsilon v_s}/(d\cosh\varepsilon)\). The uniform law \(Q(s)=1/d\) is a reference distribution; it need not be the mixture of the \(P_v\). Let \(V\) be uniformly distributed over the selected vectors and \(S_{1:n}\) be \(n\) independent observations drawn from \(P_V\). For a finite trajectory space, maximize \(\sum_\tau r(\tau)(P(\tau)-Q(\tau))\) coordinatewise to obtain

checks.claim: Final data-dependent posterior obeys a deterministic conditional-population-KL oracle inequality Eq19.
checks.explanation: The posterior depends on the same observations being averaged. A pointwise training log-loss inequality cannot be turned into a conditional-population inequality while holding that fitted posterior fixed. A positive-probability sample can select a predictor with much worse population KL than the best comparator.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(H=1\), \(P^\star=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.8)\), \(\Pi_0=\{\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.1),\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.9)\}\), and use the uniform prior. The truth is outside the model class, as Lemma 3 requires. The finite class has an exact cover, all probabilities are positive, and Assumption 1 holds with \(G=\log8\). For \(n=100\) zero observations, an event of probability \(0.2^{100}>0\), the posterior predictive success probability is
\[\widehat p=0.1+\frac{0.8}{1+9^{100}}.\]
It follows that \(\operatorname{KL}(0.8\|\widehat p)\approx1.362738\), whereas the comparator \(0.9\) gives
\[\operatorname{KL}(0.8\|0.9)+\frac{\log2}{100}\approx0.0513345.\]
The strict inequality persists for sufficiently small positive cover radius. A deterministic bound must also hold on this positive-probability event.
checks.repair:
Replace the deterministic population assertion with a proved probabilistic or expected guarantee for a specified learner. For example, on a finite positive-probability class of \(M\) distributions, let \(q_{i-1}\) be the Bayesian predictive mixture trained only on observations \(1,\ldots,i-1\), and set \(\bar q=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n q_{i-1}\). The product of the sequential predictive probabilities equals the prior mixture likelihood, so for every fixed comparator \(Q\),
\[\sum_{i=1}^n-\log q_{i-1}(S_i)\leq\sum_{i=1}^n-\log Q(S_i)+\log M.\]
For independent observations, conditioning on the past and then taking expectations gives \(n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E\operatorname{KL}(P^\star\|q_{i-1})\leq\operatorname{KL}(P^\star\|Q)+\log M/n\). Convexity in the second KL argument yields
\[\mathbb E\operatorname{KL}(P^\star\|\bar q)\leq\min_Q\operatorname{KL}(P^\star\|Q)+\frac{\log M}{n}.\]
This is an expected guarantee for a mixture of sequential predictors. It does not establish equation (19) for the final batch posterior; retaining that learner requires a separate valid generalization argument.
checks.scope: The deterministic population bound in Lemma 3 is false, including in its one-step specialization under the stated hypotheses. The example does not refute a weaker high-probability main theorem, which can allow an exceptional training event. The repair changes both the learner and the quantifier, so it cannot be substituted silently into the existing proof.

checks.demonstration:
The proof sets \(\varepsilon^2=(G^2/16)\log M/n\) and ends with \(H\varepsilon^2/4\). Substitution gives
\[\frac{HG^2\log M}{64n}=\frac{G^2\log|\Pi|}{64n},\]
whereas the theorem uses \(HG^2\log|\Pi|/(64n)\) when claiming the constant \(1/64\). For \(H=10\), \(M=4\), \(G=1\), and \(n=10000\), the full class has \(4^{10}\) elements and the two expressions differ by a factor of ten. The main text itself states \(\log|\Pi|=H\log|\Pi_0|\) immediately before Theorem 4.2.
checks.repair:
Use \(HG^2\log M/n\) with \(M\) explicitly denoting the one-step class size, or \(G^2\log|\Pi|/n\) with the full class size. A valid product construction establishes this corrected order. For \(M\geq4\), \(0<G\leq1\), and \(n\geq\log M\), set \(\varepsilon=(G/4)\sqrt{\log M/n}\). Choose \(M\) balanced orthogonal sign vectors from a sufficiently large Hadamard matrix and define \(P_v(s)=e^{\varepsilon v_s}/(d\cosh\varepsilon)\). Distinct models have KL \(\varepsilon\tanh\varepsilon\geq\varepsilon^2/2\); relative to the uniform reference, KL is at most \(\varepsilon^2/2\). Use independent uniform model indices at the \(H\) coordinates. Observations from other coordinates contain no information about a coordinate's index, so its mutual information is at most \(n\varepsilon^2/2\). Fano's inequality gives error probability at least \(1-1/32-1/2=15/32\geq1/4\) at each coordinate. Additivity of KL then yields
\[\inf_{\widehat\pi}\sup_{\pi^\star\in\Pi}\mathbb E\operatorname{KL}(P^{\pi^\star}\|P^{\widehat\pi})\geq\frac{HG^2\log M}{128n}=\frac{G^2\log|\Pi|}{128n}.\]

checks.location: Appendix K, between Eq. (2) and Eq. (3)
checks.claim: The mean-field recurrence for the expected fraction x_i (fixed point 1/4) lower-bounds the expected number of golden-path particles by B/4, and a Chernoff bound then gives per-depth loss probability at most exp(-cB), yielding O(D log(D/delta)) cost.
checks.explanation: The recurrence describes a ratio of expected counts, rather than the expectation of the random resampling ratio. Its fixed point does not establish the claimed finite-population expectation bound. Concentration must be applied conditionally to the actual population and its resampling step.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(B=1\) and an interior depth \(i\). The particle remains on the spine only if all \(i\) branch choices follow it; once it enters a trap, cloning cannot return it to the spine. Its expected spine count is therefore \(2^{-i}\), which at depth three is \(1/8<B/4\). Thus the unconditional expectation floor used in the proof is false.

More generally, condition on \(k>0\) spine particles. Let \(W\sim\operatorname{Bin}(k,1/2)\) count the offspring that continue on the spine and \(L\sim\operatorname{Bin}(B-k,1/3)\) count surviving trap particles. In an interior step, the expected next spine fraction is
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{W}{k+L}\right],\]
not \(\mathbb EW/(k+\mathbb EL)\). For example, \(B=2,k=1\) gives \(5/12\) for the former and \(3/8\) for the latter. A bound on an unconditional mean would also be insufficient on its own to establish the stated exponentially small extinction probability.
checks.repair:
Maintain the weaker high-probability invariant \(K_i\geq B/8\), where \(K_i\) is the spine count. Conditional on \(K_i=k\geq B/8\), independent branch draws give, except with probability at most \(2e^{-B/40000}\),
\[W\geq0.49k,\qquad L\leq(B-k)/3+0.01B.\]
On this event the fraction of survivors on the spine is at least
\[\frac{W}{k+L}\geq\frac{147}{1024}>\frac18.\]
The following resampling uses independent draws, so another Hoeffding bound preserves \(K_{i+1}\geq B/8\) with failure probability at most \(e^{-B/40000}\). Terminal trap deaths only improve this lower bound. Starting from \(K_0=B\), the invariant is needed only through the non-leaf spine node \(v_D\). Its next forced move visits the deepest leaf before pruning. A union bound over at most \(D\) branching and resampling steps has failure probability at most \(3D e^{-B/40000}\), so success probability is at least \(1-\delta\) when
\[B\geq\left\lceil40000\log\frac{3(D+1)}\delta\right\rceil.\]
This recovers the claimed asymptotic cost, with unoptimized constants, using the actual finite-population process.
checks.scope: The stated expectation recurrence and its use in the published concentration argument need correction. The one-particle example does not refute the logarithmic-population cost bound; the conditional argument above supplies a repair under independent branch choices and resampling.
checks.contextBefore: Starting from $x_{0}=1$ , this recurrence produces: $1\to 1/2\to 3/8\to 9/28\to\cdots$ , converging monotonically from above to the fixed point $x^{*}=1/4$ . Since the map $f(x)=\frac{3x}{2+4x}$ is strictly increasing with $f(1/4)=1/4$ , the sequence remains above $1/4$ for all $i$ . This is the key insight: because traps kill particles at rate $2/3$ per step while the golden path kills none, GWTW automatically maintains at least $25\%$ of its population on the correct path, regardless of the exponential volume of the traps.
